newsitem.title: BULGARIA: Bulgarian Socialists withdraw support for reforms.
newsitem.headline: Bulgarian Socialists withdraw support for reforms.

text.p: Bulgaria's former ruling Socialists have withdrawn their support from the interim cabinet, complaining of a lack of transparency over a new IMF accord and politically-motivated sackings of state employees.

The news, less than two weeks before elections, and at the start of a week in which donors meet in Brussels and the standby accord goes before the IMF board for approval, is a blow to President Petar Stoyanov's efforts to keep up political consensus on measures to fight severe economic crisis.

In an open letter to Stoyanov published by Bulgarian newspapers on Monday, Bulgarian Socialist Party (BSP) leader Georgi Parvanov said an all-party agreement which ended a month of street protests led by the Union of Democratic Forces (UDF) was not being respected.
"The UDF betrayed the principles agreed to lead the country out of crisis. The caretaker cabinet and yourself openly ignored those principles in your activity," Parvanov said.

The Socialists agreed on February 4 to abandon attempts to form a new government. Stoyanov appointed a caretaker cabinet, which contains many UDF members, to rule until elections on April 19 and to negotiate with the IMF.
"At this stage the BSP still has not received the text of the accord between the interim government and the IMF," Parvanov said.
He said details of the accord, which will include a tough fixed exchange rate regime, were unclear, and Bulgarians did not realise the high social cost of the reforms.

"Fragments of this document were published in the press and they confirmed that it is not clear how structural reform will be implemented and the perspectives for development of the banking sector are gloomy," Parvanov said.

"The prices of energy, fuel, transport and communications seem to be unbearable. It is true that short-term measures included in the accord envisage support for the functioning of the Bulgarian economy which is 'filling the holes', but this cannot stop but only postpone the Albanisation of our country."

The BSP won elections in December 1994 but its support evaporated as the economy plunged deeper into crisis. The Organisation for Economic Cooperation and Development forecasts annual inflation for this year at 2,000 percent.
The Group of 24 industrialised nations meet in Brussels on Tuesday and Wednesday to discuss extra support for Bulgaria, and the standby accord goes before the IMF board on Friday.

IMF Managing Director Michel Camdessus last week praised the interim cabinet's efforts to clear up the mess left by previous governments' lack of commitment to reform, saying in Moscow: "A new government is now taking courageous steps to make up for lost time -- and they lost time".
Parvanov said sackings of directors of companies and government departments had been politically motivated.
"Most of the people that were sacked were not even BSP members, they were just professionals, and we cannot say the same about the newly-appointed directors who are mainly 'blue activists,'" he said.

"We are worried by the fact that in some spheres, especially in the tourist business, we have new faces connected to strong-arm (criminal) groups, which is maybe an attempt to reward their efforts in the January unrest."

Parvanov met Stoyanov last month to express his concern. Stoyanov said dismissals were motivated purely by considerations of efficiency and competence, and in his view the measures by the interim cabinet did not go far enough.

Leading BSP figures told Troud daily they had not been told about the letter, which was a personal initiative of Parvanov, who took over as Socialist leader in December after the resignation of former prime minister Zhan Videnov.
An opinion poll released by Gallup on Friday showed support of 60 to 62 percent for the UDF and its coalition allies, and support for the Socialists at 16 to 17 percent.
